opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the genuinely important open questions, and it's one where I've updated a bit over time.

The basic observation is that current systems are wildly less data-efficient than humans. A human professional gets good at their job after maybe a few years of experience, which is a tiny amount of data compared to what goes into pretraining a frontier model. And humans learn continuously on the job: you make a mistake on Monday, and by Wednesday you've internalized the lesson. Current models mostly don't. They're trained, frozen, and deployed, and whatever they "learn" during deployment lives in the context window and disappears when the context ends.

So one view, which I take seriously, is that this is a real bottleneck. You can get very impressive systems that are great at short, well-specified tasks, but they'll keep hitting a wall on the long, messy, context-heavy work that makes up a lot of real jobs, especially research. On that view, progress could look like a lot of impressive benchmarks and then a frustrating plateau in actual economic impact until someone cracks continual learning.

That said, I don't think it's likely to be a long-lasting bottleneck, for a few reasons.

First, there are a lot of ways to partially route around it. Longer context windows, better memory and retrieval scaffolding, and periodic fine-tuning on deployment data all get you some of the benefit without a fundamental breakthrough. It doesn't have to be elegant to work.

Second, the companies are clearly aware of this and are pouring effort into it. Sample efficiency and online learning look to me like the kind of problem that yields to a lot of smart people and a lot of compute, not the kind that needs some deep conceptual revolution that might take decades. The human brain is an existence proof that much better data efficiency is physically possible.

Third, and this is the most important point for my forecasts: you don't necessarily need human-level data efficiency to automate AI research itself. If you get systems that are good enough coders and good enough research engineers to substantially speed up the AI companies' own work, then that acceleration gets applied to the data efficiency problem too. Then the bottleneck becomes something the AIs are helping solve, rather than something that only slow human research has to solve.

So my overall take is that limits in online learning are probably the biggest reason my timelines aren't even shorter. They add real uncertainty and could push things back by a few years. But I don't think they're a reason to expect the whole thing to stall out. If anything, I'd guess that once someone gets continual learning working well, it'll show up as a fairly sudden jump in how useful these systems are, because a lot of the remaining gap between "impressive demo" and "drop-in remote worker" is exactly this ability to learn on the job.

r001.rationale: The response says companies are already aware of the issue and are investing effort, but does not clearly predict additional effort conditional on the limitations becoming a significant bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says systems need not reach human-level data efficiency to speed up AI companies’ research work, and that this acceleration can help solve the data-efficiency problem.

r003.rationale: It notes that frontier models use far more data than humans and mentions compute as part of solving the problem, but does not argue that sufficiently large training expenditures can compensate for lower data efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the big open questions, and I think it's actually one of the main cruxes between people who expect things to go really fast over the next few years and people who think it'll be more gradual.

So the way I think about it is: current systems are incredibly data-inefficient compared to humans. A human learns to be a competent software engineer or a competent researcher with, you know, maybe a few years of relevant experience, a modest amount of reading, a lot of trial and error on the job. A frontier model has read basically the entire internet and still, in a lot of ways, is less capable than an experienced human at doing long, messy, open-ended projects. And a big part of that is the online learning piece. When a human starts a new job, they're bad at it for a few months, they make mistakes, they get corrected, and they just permanently get better. They remember what happened last week. Current models mostly don't do that. Each conversation is more or less a fresh start, and whatever learning happens, happens offline in big training runs with lots of lag.

Now, there are two ways this could go. One story is that this is a deep, hard problem, and we'll be stuck with systems that are very impressive at narrow tasks but just can't accumulate the kind of tacit, on-the-job knowledge that makes a senior person senior. In that world, I'd expect progress to be slower and bumpier than what I've written about, because you don't get the automated AI researcher that actually gets better at research over time, you get a very good assistant that keeps plateauing on anything long-horizon.

The other story, which I find somewhat more likely, is that this is more of an engineering bottleneck than a fundamental one. We already see partial workarounds — long contexts, retrieval, scaffolding that writes notes to itself, continual fine-tuning on the model's own trajectories — and these are kind of clunky, but they're improving. And more importantly, the labs know this is the bottleneck. When a bottleneck is well-identified and lots of smart people with lots of compute are attacking it, my prior is that it tends to get solved, often faster than outside observers expect. If you look at the history of the field, things like "models can't do math" or "models can't use tools" were treated as deep limitations and then became fairly ordinary engineering problems once there was enough pressure on them.

The thing I'd really emphasize, though, is that even if data efficiency stays bad relative to humans, that may not matter as much as people think. Because the comparison that matters isn't "one AI versus one human." It's "a very large number of AI copies running in parallel at very high speed versus a human research team." If you can run a hundred thousand instances and they can share what they learn through some mechanism — even a crude one — then you can afford to be quite data-inefficient per instance and still outpace humans in aggregate. Humans can't do that. I can't copy my experience directly into your head.

So my honest view is something like: online learning and data efficiency are probably the main reason timelines could be longer than I expect. If I'm wrong about fast progress, this is likely where I'm wrong. But I don't think it's the kind of thing that pushes us out to decades. It feels more like the kind of thing that could add a couple of years, and that might be the difference between, say, 2027 and 2029 or 2030, rather than the difference between "soon" and "never." And frankly, a couple of extra years would be really valuable from a safety and governance standpoint, so I'd be very happy to be wrong in that direction.

r001.rationale: It says that once labs identify this as a bottleneck, many people with substantial compute will work on it, and that such bottlenecks tend to get solved.

r002.rationale: It says many AI copies running in parallel could outpace a human research team despite poor per-instance data efficiency, but does not clearly claim that automating most AI research would drive that acceleration.

r003.rationale: It discusses parallel AI instances compensating for poor data efficiency, but does not claim that large training expenditures would compensate for it.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re important limitations, but I’m uncertain about how much they’ll slow things down. I’d distinguish between a capability that current systems are missing and a bottleneck that will take a long time to overcome. Online learning and data efficiency are clearly areas where we’d like systems to do better; that doesn’t by itself tell us how hard the improvements will be.

For online learning, there’s a difference between learning something during a conversation and having that learning persist, so that the system becomes a better worker over weeks or months. If you have to keep teaching it the same things, that’s a substantial disadvantage. It makes it harder to substitute for someone who accumulates experience on the job. But you can get some of the benefits through memory and by periodically training on experience, even without solving continuous learning in a completely general way.

Data efficiency matters especially when the experience you need is expensive or slow to obtain. If a system needs enormous numbers of examples to learn a task, and each example requires a real-world experiment, that could really slow progress. In domains where you can generate experience cheaply and check whether you succeeded, the constraint may be much weaker.

So my expectation would be uneven progress. These limitations could hold back some applications quite a lot while allowing rapid progress in others. And the question I’d particularly want to answer is whether they prevent AI systems from substantially accelerating AI research. If they don’t, then they might be important shortcomings without buying us much additional time.

r001.rationale: The response describes online learning and data efficiency as possible bottlenecks but does not predict that companies will devote more effort to improving them.

r002.rationale: It asks whether limitations would prevent AI systems from accelerating AI research, but does not propose that automating most AI research could accelerate progress without substantial improvements in these areas.

r003.rationale: The response discusses the cost of obtaining examples but does not argue that sufficiently large training expenditures could offset lower data efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are real limitations, but I’m uncertain how much they’ll slow things down. It helps to separate two questions: how quickly we can train more capable models, and how quickly those models can learn to do something useful once they’re deployed.

You could have a model that’s very impressive on a wide range of tasks but can’t learn from experience in the way a human employee does. You explain something to it, it does some work, you give it feedback — and then tomorrow you’re having to explain the same thing again. That would make it much harder to automate jobs that require accumulating lots of context and adapting to a particular organisation.

But that doesn’t necessarily stop progress in the underlying models. You can still train the next model on more data, including data generated by earlier models. And some apparent online learning can happen through context: you give the model a record of what happened previously, and it adjusts its behaviour without changing its weights.

The question is how far those substitutes get you. If improving further requires lots of fresh experience in the real world, and that experience is expensive or takes a long time to collect, then data efficiency could become a serious bottleneck. If models can learn a lot from relatively little feedback, or generate useful training experience in environments you can run very quickly, then it’s much less of a constraint.

So I’d put some probability on this substantially slowing progress. But I wouldn’t feel comfortable counting on it to give us a long time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data efficiency as a possible bottleneck but does not predict that companies will devote more effort to improving it.

r002.rationale: It says later models can train on more data, including model-generated data, but does not propose automating most AI research as a way to accelerate progress.

r003.rationale: It notes that fresh real-world experience could be costly and slow to collect, but does not argue that sufficiently large training expenditures could offset lower data efficiency than humans.
